exam: A 45‑year‑old woman post‑mastectomy presents with hot flashes; what is the most appropriate next step? — Reassure, offer non‑hormonal measures; continue tamoxifen unless severe.

How does tamoxifen differ from aromatase inhibitors in mechanism and side‑effects? — Blocks estrogen receptor vs blocks estrogen synthesis; tamoxifen causes uterine effects and VTE, aromatase inhibitors cause osteoporosis.
A patient on tamoxifen develops new vaginal bleeding; what should you do? — Rule out endometrial pathology with ultrasound or referral; consider stopping tamoxifen if cancer risk high.
Why is tamoxifen preferred over aromatase inhibitors in pre‑menopausal women? — Aromatase inhibitors require ovarian suppression; tamoxifen works without suppressing ovarian function.
What monitoring is essential before starting tamoxifen in a low‑resource setting? — Baseline liver function, pregnancy test, and assessment for thrombotic risk.
A patient on tamoxifen presents with leg swelling; what is the immediate management? — Assess for DVT using clinical scoring; start anticoagulation if high probability and no contraindication.
Explain the rationale for extending tamoxifen therapy to 10 years in high‑risk patients. — Longer duration reduces recurrence and mortality without markedly increasing serious adverse events.
What drug interactions should be avoided with tamoxifen? — Strong CYP2D6 inhibitors (e.g., fluoxetine) reduce its activation; avoid concomitant use.
ai.title: Tamoxifen in Breast Cancer Management
ai.subject: Pharmacology
ai.summary: Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator used mainly for estrogen‑receptor positive breast cancer. It works by blocking estrogen in breast tissue while acting as an agonist in bone and uterus. Understanding its indications, monitoring, and side‑effects is essential for low‑resource settings.

b: Indicated for adjuvant therapy, neoadjuvant therapy, and metastatic ER‑positive breast cancer
Also used for chemoprevention in high‑risk women
sections.p: Tamoxifen blocks estrogen receptors in breast tissue, preventing tumour growth in ER‑positive cancers. It is oral, inexpensive and widely available, making it a cornerstone therapy in many African hospitals.

b: Mechanism: competitive antagonist at estrogen receptor α in breast, partial agonist in uterus and bone
Half‑life ~5‑7 days; steady state reached after 4‑6 weeks
sections.p: Tamoxifen’s mixed agonist/antagonist activity explains its benefits and risks. In bone it preserves density; in uterus it can stimulate endometrial growth, raising cancer risk.

b: Start after surgery or when systemic therapy is indicated
Continue for 5‑10 years depending on risk and tolerance
sections.p: In low‑resource settings, tamoxifen often replaces more costly aromatase inhibitors. Monitoring relies on clinical assessment and basic labs rather than expensive imaging.
